sections.content:
This course serves as an introduction to probability and statistics. It also introduces R to perform the tasks in each of the topics.

Topics:
Descriptive statistics
- Graphical summaries: Frequency table, Histogram, Line Chart, Pie chart, Box plot
- Definitions of data, experiment, variables, observation
- Different types of data
- Mean, median, mode, trimmed mean
- Quantiles, Quartiles, Interquartile range, Variance, Standard deviation

Probability:
- Definitions of sample space and events
- Operations of sets/events: union, intersection, complement and difference
- Associative, Distributive and De Morgan's law of events
- Probability: definition and properties
- Counting techniques and permutations and combinations
- Conditional Probability
- Independence
- Total Probability and Bayes' Theorem

Random Variables
- Discrete Random Variables: pmf, cdf, E(X) and Var(X) (including linear combinations of random variables)
- Continuous Random Variables: pdf, cdf, E(X) and Var(X) (including linear combinations of random variables), finding cdf of a related variable (e.g. cdf of Y = X^2 from cdf of X), Chebyshev's Theorem
- Some common probability distributions: Binomial, Poisson and Normal/Gaussian

Estimation
- Estimator vs Estimate
- Point Estimation Basics: Bias, Variance, MSE (including proofs)
- Unbiased estimators of population mean and variance
- Methods of point Estimation: MME and MLE

=== Midterm ===

Estimation (continued)
- Sampling distributions and interval estimation
- Confidence interval of population mean with known population variance and normal distribution
- Confidence interval of population mean with unknown population variance and normal distribution (i.e. t distribution)
- Confidence interval of population variance from normal distribution (using chi-squared distribution)

Hypothesis Testing
- Basics: Null hypothesis, alternative hypothesis, one sided vs two sided test, significance level, Type I and Type II error, power
- Different methods of hypothesis testing: using critical values, critical regions and p-values
- Hypothesis test of population mean with known population variance and normal distribution (i.e. z-test)
- Hypothesis test of population mean with unknown population variance and normal distribution (i.e. t-test)
- Hypothesis test of population variance from normal distribution (using chi-squared distribution)
- Relationship between two sided hypothesis tests and confidence intervals
- Calculation of power of tests

ANOVA
- Two sample z-test with known population variances
- Two sample t-test with unknown equal population variance.
- Two sample t-test with unknown unequal population variances (i.e. Welch's t-test)
- Different types of variances: SST, SSTreat and SSE and their relation
- ANOVA: assumptions and methodology
- Welch's ANOVA
- Relationship between ANOVA and two sample t-test
- Tuckey's HSD

Linear Regression:
- Basic linear regression model
- Least square estimators of gradient and intercept
- Unbiasedness of least square estimators
- Variance of least square estimators
- Confidence intervals and hypothesis testing of least square estimators
- SST, RSS and SSE
- R^2 and Pearson's linear correlation coefficient
- Strength, sign and quality of linear regression

=== Finals ===

Overall the content is quite solid for an introductory statistics course. It would be even better if it included goodness of fit test and non parametric methods (which are included in some semesters) but the syllabus is already huge as is if you have no statistics background, so I'd say this much is fair.

My Grade: A+

Now why did I give grading a D. Well its because the assessments were terrible.

First lets talk about homework. All homeworks have an online quiz (10 MCQs worth 4 points each) and a 60 mark written part. The grades of the online quizzes were legit released after the finals. Like wtf it would have been nice to review any mistakes made in them. The feedback for written homework was also usually delivered late with no comments.

Now lets talk about the exams. For some fucking reason, calculators were not allowed in either exam (I genuinely have no clue why). Don't worry, questions were set such that they were possible without a calculator. Now this wasn't much of a problem for midterm, as with the given topics, you can ask quite a few questions that do not need use of calculator.

The problem was the finals. Of course, doing hypothesis tests is not possible without calculators so the types of questions that could be set are very limited. Writing R code is not tested in exams but analysing outputs from R to perform tests is included. This lead to a paper that was wayyyy too easy as all we had to do is copy the output from R and make conclusions. Well, at least for the first 86 marks. The last 14 marks was a linear regression proof that I believe very few people (like maybe 5 or 6) could do because holy fuck what was that. Therefore I'll guess that for the final exams the mean, median, upper and lower quartiles were all probably extremely similar. This meant that making a small silly mistake probably lead to falling behind many grades (unless you were able to the last question, in which case guaranteed A+ honestly).

Exams should not be set like this. Exams should have questions of varying difficulty to allow students of different abilities to be distinguished. The finals (worth 60% mind you) was insultingly easy for 86 marks and mind fuckingly difficult for 14 marks. This all could have been avoided if they simply allowed calculators for the exam, which would have allowed for more types of question to be asked, instead of this "R-output analysis" exam we got.

Solve basic problems in probability.

Make inferences about the population by applying suitable statistical approaches, such as estimation, hypothesis testing, and linear regression.

Formulate statistical questions for real-world problems and interpret the results.

Analyze data using R.

概率论简介(introduction to probability theory): 加法原理、乘法原理、排列组合、古典概型、条件概率、全概率公式、贝叶斯公式等

假设检验: 零假设和备择假设、第一类错误和第二类错误、临界值法和p值法、简单检验和复合检验(单侧检验(右侧检验和左侧检验)和双侧检验)

[with EASY single var Calculus]

[learn how to identify when use which distribution]

i)  Point Estimator: Biasness, Precision, Goodness of point est.
[Use many E(x), Var(x)]

[Z,T,Chi-squared, basically refer to these 3 distribution tables]

------- Midterm -------

i) Null(Ho) vs Alternative(H1), Type 1 & Type 2 Errors, Power
[Reject or NOT reject Ho, One-sided(>or<), Two-sided(!=), simple]
ii) Z,T,Chi-squared Test using Ho & H1
**[Concept same as C.I. (Chap 4ii)]**

6. Simple Linear Regression
- Linear regression
**[Use your calculator and programs]**

7. Two Sample Testing
- Concept same as Chap 5, but analyze 2 variables
[Added F Distribution and F tables]

- Compare significance difference in variances for >2 populations
[USE CALCULATOR PROGRAM, DON'T WASTE TIME!]

- Fundamentals of set theory
- Basic combinatorics and probability, e.g., Counting, multiplication rule, independent events, conditional probability, Bayes' theorem

This course is called APPLIED statistics.

sections.content:
Before midterm: Probability and some basic statistical concepts like mean and sd. After midtem: distributions, hypothesis testing, estimation, linear regression.

Concepts are relatively easy to understand. To solve questions on the exam you just need to know how to use formulas most of the time. Cheatsheet is allowed on the final exam.

You also need to remember the R-codes, which is essentially a statistical programming language (just basic ones).

For a lot of problems you need to type a lot of data into the calculator, so a minor mistake can lead to a whole question wrong, which is stupid in my opinion. Using a more sophisticated calculator might be advantageous
sections.teaching:
Rarely attended class, because it is pretty boring. The teacher is okay, but the lecture is not efficient.

Review questions are very important to be understood, because the exams are based on them. Some exam questions are almost identical to the review ones. Review questions are covered only in class so make sure you get the solutions somehow.
sections.grading:
Grading is fair, overall mean was 71, sd 19. Since the material is relatively easy, this course could help you raise your gpa, if you put enough time into it.

Your final grade is counted by 40-60 or 0-100 scheme depending on whichever gives you a higher result
sections.workload: The workload is not that hard. You don't have to be smart in order to succeed in it, since it doesn't make you think and analyze. You generally just need to know how to use the formulas and solve review questions.
